question: What should come in the place of blank number 3?
solution:
The correct answer is '**outcomes**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In ethics, **consequentialism** evaluates actions by their **results**; hence the standard is the net **outcomes**.
 
• The blank asks what consequentialism judges by; “**outcomes**” precisely matches the theory’s core idea.
 
• Terms like “goods” or “benefits” are one-sided (only positives), whereas consequentialism weighs **both benefits and harms**.
 
• “Profit” is narrowly financial and not appropriate for a general **moral philosophy** context.

Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

Complete Passage: *Modern ethical debates tend to concern the conflict between deontological and consequentialist approaches, each providing a (1) rigorous__ methodology. Deontology requires respect for moral (2) __actions__ irrespective of the result, while consequentialism judges on the basis of the net (3) __outcomes__. Objections against pure consequentialism suggest it will allow **(4) __immoral__** actions if these bring about maximum overall welfare. In reply, some recommend __(5) well balanced__ hybrid theories that combine obligations with outcome sensitivity*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Goods**: Implies only positive values; consequentialism considers the **total balance** of good and bad results.
 
• **Benefits**: One-sided; ignores potential **costs/harms** that are also weighed in consequentialist evaluation.
 
• **Profit**: A financial term; too narrow for general ethical assessment of actions in moral philosophy.
